justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level of the underlying asset at the time of the forecast, with a modest upward drift built in across horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I assumed mean-reverting behavior around the recent trading range, with little expected directional movement given the absence of imminent catalysts. The 1-week estimate incorporated a slight upward bias reflecting the general tendency of risk assets to trend modestly higher over short horizons in the absence of negative shocks, while the 1-month estimate extended that drift further but remained close to the near-term anchor, reflecting the idea that over medium horizons, prices tend to revert toward fair value estimates rather than extrapolate short-term momentum aggressively.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each respective time horizon. For the 1-day interval, realized intraday volatility provided a relatively tight bound, as price movements over a single session tend to cluster within a predictable range under normal market conditions. As the horizon extended to one week and then one month, I widened the intervals to reflect the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty, as well as the compounding possibility of regime changes, shifting macro narratives, and liquidity conditions that become increasingly relevant over longer periods.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a worse-than-expected inflation print or a sharp rise in unemployment — could trigger a risk-off selloff that breaks the lower bound of even the 1-month interval. A geopolitical shock or financial contagion event would have similar effects. On the upside, an unexpected dovish pivot from a major central bank, stronger-than-anticipated earnings, or a significant short-squeeze could push prices well above the upper confidence bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging model uncertainty itself as a source of tail risk. These intervals assume that the underlying statistical relationships governing price behavior remain stable, but structural breaks — such as a fundamental change in market microstructure, a major policy announcement, or a black swan event — can render historically calibrated intervals deeply misleading. The stated 90% confidence intervals should be understood as conditional on roughly normal market functioning, and investors should maintain awareness that the true probability of exceeding these bounds may be higher than the label implies.
